subject: WSJ Travel: No More Passport Application Hassles? 📋

96 Plus, Alaska woos big spenders, and United brings basic fares to first class   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Dawn Gilbertson   Need a Passport? Things Should Get Easier Next Year   Plus, Alaska woos big spenders, and United brings basic fares to first class   Happy Friday! I’m just back from Washington state and can’t stop raving about the beauty of the Olympic Peninsula. I traveled 500 miles from Seattle to Lake Crescent in Olympic National Park, Cape Flattery and more for an upcoming column.  

   In Seattle, I attended Alaska Airlines’ investor and media day. The hometown carrier, lagging behind its larger rivals in the push for big-spending travelers, showed off new business-class suites, its first premium-economy section and new lounges . Get ready to hear Aurora a lot. That’s the new name for its business-class cabin with dedicated airport check-in, security and an exclusive lounge. If you think that sounds a lot like Delta One, American Flagship and United’s Polaris, you’re right.  

   Wish I’d had time to check out Amtrak’s newest train, Airo, launched this week on the Cascade route in the Pacific Northwest. Amtrak offers four daily trips between Vancouver, British Columbia, Seattle, Portland and Eugene, Ore. 

   The biggest travel news this week was the horrifying cockpit stabbing and plane nosedive on a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel.  

   United Airlines said it’s bringing those dreaded basic fares to first class. You already know how I feel about this trend .  

   And Vail Resorts telegraphed another weak ski season with season-pass sales through Sept. 18 down 12% from a year ago. 

       Fewer complications?     JENNY KANE/ASSOCIATED PRESS   Applying for a passport is both exciting and exhausting. The government this week announced plans to smooth the application process, which today requires several steps including an in-person appointment. 

   Travelers will be able to apply online beginning next year , Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. When next year? No one’s saying yet. You can already renew passports online in many cases. 

   Another improvement on the way: No more drugstore photos required. You’ll be able to snap a selfie. In his prepared remarks, Rubio called the drugstore shots “hostage” photos.

   “You probably can’t use those filters to make you look 50 years younger, but you can take a picture of yourself on the phone in the comfort of your home, or you can upload one directly from your own device,” he said.

   One of the big reasons for the change, besides the fact that it’s 2026 and we can do almost everything online: all the pricey passport services that have cropped up to help travelers navigate the application maze.

   Today, Rubio said, there’s “an entire cottage industry that’s built around cashing in on every stage of the passport process.” You probably know someone who has been tricked by all those sponsored ads, or have applied through a for-profit company yourself.

   The new system will also feature real-time status updates so you don’t have to keep checking your mailbox ahead of an international trip. Stay tuned for more details.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Travel newsletter, a weekly source of inspiration and advice for navigating your vacations and business trips, along with the latest travel news. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       Notes From the Road ✈️     LIAM EISENBERG FOR WSJ   • Don’t let those premium credit-card perks go to waste. Here’s how I shaved hundreds off two luxury hotel stays .

   • Our tech columnist used Meta’s Muse to collect Global Entry application documents . 

   • What it’s like to fly Alaska Airlines’ business class . 

   • Would you go on safari in an Uber ? The ride-share company’s experiment in Nairobi is already stumbling.

   • Don’t let a lack of nonstop flights deter you: The Seychelles has a decadent crop of luxury retreats .

       MEMBER MESSAGE: MARKETWATCH PICKS     I’m 62 With $7M. Where can I find one?   READ MORE  >       Travel Math 🧮   1.1 million   The number of annual passholders at Disneyland, according to former CEO Bob Chapek’s memoir. Disney has traditionally kept membership figures for its Magic Key program private.

       And We Quote 💬   “The first time I met him, I asked him, ‘Why did your parents name you the smiling mosquito?’” 

   —Gurucharan Arora on the 38-year-old FlyDubai Captain, Smit Machchhar, being hailed as a hero . Smit means smiling and his last name means mosquito, Arora said. He supervised Machchhar during his early career training at SpiceJet.

       You Have Thoughts 🤔   …on babies in business class : 

   • “Your hack regarding buying a business class seat for one parent on long flights brought back a very unpleasant experience flying Denver to Honolulu years ago. Having splurged for first-class tickets, my wife and I watched the senior couple in the seats across from us bring their toddler and infant grandchildren up from economy to spare the children’s parents. The parents may have had a quiet flight but the passengers in first class didn’t. Thanks, Grandma and Grandpa .” — Jeff Ricketts, Florida 

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.) 

       Cheers and Jeers 🤷   Big cheers to TSA PreCheck Touchless ID . Yes, I’m becoming a broken record on this, but it saved me line angst again this week. Seattle-Tacoma International Airport was surprisingly busy for a random weekday in late September. There were more than two dozen passengers in the PreCheck lane and a 39-minute wait for standard security screening. There was one person in the Touchless line and I breezed through.

   Cheers to Alaska Airlines for proactively offering to change passengers’ seats on a less-than-full flight from Phoenix to Seattle last weekend. A gate agent made the announcement just before boarding and told interested passengers to come up to the counter. It was a first for me.

   Jeers to yet another flight with flimsy power outlets. My phone charger on the Alaska flight kept falling out and I was on a newer plane. There was no USB-C option, unfortunately. I have a portable charger but save it for places without outlets.

       In My Carry-on 👜     ALASKA AIRLINES   Alaska Airlines CEO Ben Minicucci is an avid cyclist. So he packs his Lake bike shoes to use in the hotel gym. 

   He hops on a Peloton or other spin bike and works out for an hour. And if he forgets his bike shoes? He goes barefoot or puts on his dress shoes.

   “I look really weird but it’s four in the morning,” says Minicucci. “Nobody’s there.”

       One Final Shot 📷     DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ   I made it to Olympic National Park in Washington in time for sunset from Lake Crescent Lodge.

Dawn Gilbertson
 
Need a Passport? Things Should Get Easier Next Year
 
Plus, Alaska woos big spenders, and United brings basic fares to first class
 

Happy Friday! I’m just back from Washington state and can’t stop raving about the beauty of the Olympic Peninsula. I traveled 500 miles from Seattle to Lake Crescent in Olympic National Park, Cape Flattery and more for an upcoming column. 

 

In Seattle, I attended Alaska Airlines’ investor and media day. The hometown carrier, lagging behind its larger rivals in the push for big-spending travelers, showed off new business-class suites, its first premium-economy section and new lounges. Get ready to hear Aurora a lot. That’s the new name for its business-class cabin with dedicated airport check-in, security and an exclusive lounge. If you think that sounds a lot like Delta One, American Flagship and United’s Polaris, you’re right. 

 

Wish I’d had time to check out Amtrak’s newest train, Airo, launched this week on the Cascade route in the Pacific Northwest. Amtrak offers four daily trips between Vancouver, British Columbia, Seattle, Portland and Eugene, Ore.

 

The biggest travel news this week was the horrifying cockpit stabbing and plane nosedive on a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel. 

 

United Airlines said it’s bringing those dreaded basic fares to first class. You already know how I feel about this trend. 

 

And Vail Resorts telegraphed another weak ski season with season-pass sales through Sept. 18 down 12% from a year ago.

 
 
 

Fewer complications?

 
 
JENNY KANE/ASSOCIATED PRESS
 

Applying for a passport is both exciting and exhausting. The government this week announced plans to smooth the application process, which today requires several steps including an in-person appointment. 

 

Travelers will be able to apply online beginning next year, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. When next year? No one’s saying yet. You can already renew passports online in many cases. 

 

Another improvement on the way: No more drugstore photos required. You’ll be able to snap a selfie. In his prepared remarks, Rubio called the drugstore shots “hostage” photos.

 

“You probably can’t use those filters to make you look 50 years younger, but you can take a picture of yourself on the phone in the comfort of your home, or you can upload one directly from your own device,” he said.

 

One of the big reasons for the change, besides the fact that it’s 2026 and we can do almost everything online: all the pricey passport services that have cropped up to help travelers navigate the application maze.

 

Today, Rubio said, there’s “an entire cottage industry that’s built around cashing in on every stage of the passport process.” You probably know someone who has been tricked by all those sponsored ads, or have applied through a for-profit company yourself.

 

The new system will also feature real-time status updates so you don’t have to keep checking your mailbox ahead of an international trip. Stay tuned for more details.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ Travel newsletter, a weekly source of inspiration and advice for navigating your vacations and business trips, along with the latest travel news. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

Notes From the Road ✈️

 
 
LIAM EISENBERG FOR WSJ
 

• Don’t let those premium credit-card perks go to waste. Here’s how I shaved hundreds off two luxury hotel stays.

 

• Our tech columnist used Meta’s Muse to collect Global Entry application documents. 

 

• What it’s like to fly Alaska Airlines’ business class. 

 

• Would you go on safari in an Uber? The ride-share company’s experiment in Nairobi is already stumbling.

 

• Don’t let a lack of nonstop flights deter you: The Seychelles has a decadent crop of luxury retreats.

Travel Math 🧮

 
1.1 million
 

The number of annual passholders at Disneyland, according to former CEO Bob Chapek’s memoir. Disney has traditionally kept membership figures for its Magic Key program private.

 
 
 

And We Quote 💬

 

“The first time I met him, I asked him, ‘Why did your parents name you the smiling mosquito?’”

 

—Gurucharan Arora on the 38-year-old FlyDubai Captain, Smit Machchhar, being hailed as a hero. Smit means smiling and his last name means mosquito, Arora said. He supervised Machchhar during his early career training at SpiceJet.

 
 
 

You Have Thoughts 🤔

 

…on babies in business class:

 

• “Your hack regarding buying a business class seat for one parent on long flights brought back a very unpleasant experience flying Denver to Honolulu years ago. Having splurged for first-class tickets, my wife and I watched the senior couple in the seats across from us bring their toddler and infant grandchildren up from economy to spare the children’s parents. The parents may have had a quiet flight but the passengers in first class didn’t. Thanks, Grandma and Grandpa .” —Jeff Ricketts, Florida

 

(Responses have been condensed and edited.)

 
 
 

Cheers and Jeers 🤷

 

Big cheers to TSA PreCheck Touchless ID. Yes, I’m becoming a broken record on this, but it saved me line angst again this week. Seattle-Tacoma International Airport was surprisingly busy for a random weekday in late September. There were more than two dozen passengers in the PreCheck lane and a 39-minute wait for standard security screening. There was one person in the Touchless line and I breezed through.

 

Cheers to Alaska Airlines for proactively offering to change passengers’ seats on a less-than-full flight from Phoenix to Seattle last weekend. A gate agent made the announcement just before boarding and told interested passengers to come up to the counter. It was a first for me.

 

Jeers to yet another flight with flimsy power outlets. My phone charger on the Alaska flight kept falling out and I was on a newer plane. There was no USB-C option, unfortunately. I have a portable charger but save it for places without outlets.

 
 
 

In My Carry-on 👜

 
 
ALASKA AIRLINES
 

Alaska Airlines CEO Ben Minicucci is an avid cyclist. So he packs his Lake bike shoes to use in the hotel gym. 

 

He hops on a Peloton or other spin bike and works out for an hour. And if he forgets his bike shoes? He goes barefoot or puts on his dress shoes.

 

“I look really weird but it’s four in the morning,” says Minicucci. “Nobody’s there.”

 
 
 

One Final Shot 📷

 
 
DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ
 

I made it to Olympic National Park in Washington in time for sunset from Lake Crescent Lodge.
